landmarkDescriptions.molassesReefLight: The reef light is the easiest above-water reference and a useful way to stay oriented around the central reef.
landmarkDescriptions.shipsWinch: A large ship's winch rests near the reef light—a compact piece of maritime history now folded into the reef.
landmarkDescriptions.spanishAnchor: An old anchor lies among the coral formations. Let the crew point it out; it can disappear surprisingly well into the reef.
landmarkDescriptions.flightDeckAndCranes: The broad flight deck and paired cranes make the ship's scale click into place. Stay outside the structure and follow the guide's line.
landmarkDescriptions.wellDeck: The open well deck is one of the wreck's most dramatic exterior spaces, with changing light and room for big schools of fish.
landmarkDescriptions.christOfAbyssStatue: The 8.6-foot bronze statue stands on a concrete pedestal in shallow water—the unmistakable centrepiece of this dive.
landmarkDescriptions.dryRocksSandChannels: Bright sand channels weave between coral formations around the statue and are good places to look for rays, grouper, and moray eels.
landmarkDescriptions.generic: A memorable reference point the crew can identify during the site briefing.

name.detail: First and last in two columns, or one full-name column — either works. This is the only thing a row truly needs.

email.detail: How DiveDay reaches a diver and recognizes a returning one, so a second import updates them instead of making a duplicate. A row without one still comes in as a new diver.

phone.detail: Mobile or landline, however you've written it.

emergencyContact.detail: A name and a phone number, when you have them, land on the diver's card.

diveInsurance.detail: However you keep it — a DAN number, a provider name — comes across as written. It's never a gate; it's what the crew wants on hand in an incident.

certification.detail: Agency, level, and card number. The card number is what lets a card come across at all — see the scope table below for how it's verified.

refresherDue.detail: If you track a refresher date, it comes across however your sheet writes dates (05/04/2030, 4-May-2030, 2030-05-04). A past date lands as a card that's due — that's the point. An unreadable date goes to staff review instead of verified.

specialty.detail: Deep, wreck, night, or drysuit — one cell can name several (“Deep, Wreck”) and each becomes its own card under the diver's agency number. See the scope table below for how it's verified.

nitrox.detail: A yes/no column, plus the nitrox card number if you keep one — that's what brings it across. See the scope table below for how a nitrox fill is gated.

rentalSizes.detail: BCD, wetsuit, boot, and fin — whatever sizes you already track become a fit profile.

pastVisits.detail: Keep a booking log? A date, trip name, and price per row becomes that diver's history here, so a regular arrives as a regular. Repeat their email on each row to match the right person. See the scope table below for what it means.

cutover.heading: Cutover without drama
cutover.intro: Leaving a system you've run for years doesn't have to mean a weekend of downtime. Here's the switch, step by step.

step1.title: Run both systems for one trip cycle
step1.detail: Import into DiveDay and start taking real trips through it — waivers, roster, manifest — while you keep your old system running alongside it. Nothing forces a hard cutoff on day one.

step2.title: Time it to your slow season
step2.detail: Pick a week with the fewest trips already on the books. Fewer live bookings straddling the switch means less to reconcile by hand.

step3.title: A second import updates your roster, it doesn't duplicate it
step3.detail: Re-run the export later, once your old system has more bookings in it. DiveDay matches existing divers by email and updates them instead of creating a second record, and a repeated visit history collapses instead of doubling.

step4.title: Budget an afternoon, not a week
step4.detail: Exporting from the old system is minutes of work, and the preview shows exactly what will land before anything saves. Review it, fix any flagged rows, import for real. One sitting, not a project plan.

item1.title: Readiness that won't let an unready diver board
item1.detail: The trip and the dive site decide what each diver needs; if a card or waiver can't be verified, DiveDay says so plainly instead of passing them through. {competitor} takes the booking — it never checks whether the diver is cleared to get on the boat.

item2.title: Certification checks that actually gate the dive
item2.detail: DiveDay gates the dive on the card: a deep dive won't clear a diver who isn't carded for it, and every nitrox fill is re-checked at fill time. Cards you enter are verified by staff; cards you bring in come across verified and flagged imported, with a one-tap confirm. A general booking engine has no concept of a C-card.

item3.title: Native waivers with medical review — in every tier
item3.detail: Waivers are built in and versioned against your own release, and a medical answer that calls for a physician's sign-off blocks the diver until that review — it doesn't just warn. Not a form stapled to a checkout, and not a paid add-on.

item4.title: A roll-call manifest that survives the dock
item4.detail: Big Boarded / Not-boarded buttons for wet thumbs, a head count for every dive, and a manifest the crew saves to the phone so it keeps working after the signal drops at the ramp.

item5.title: Rental fit and the trip's packing list
item5.detail: Every diver's sizes become the boat's kit list, with a tank per diver per dive split by air and nitrox. {competitor} doesn't know a diver's wetsuit size.

item6.title: The night-before brief and a recap they share
item6.detail: Each diver gets a plain-language brief the night before — dock time, conditions, what to bring — and a shareable recap page after. The booking confirmation was the start; this is the rest of the relationship.

eve.cardSummary: Long the Windows desktop shop-management system for PADI retailers, now owned by DiveShop360. Export your customers and cards, then bring them here.
eve.metaDescription: Leaving EVE? A step-by-step guide to exporting your customers and certifications from EVE and bringing them into DiveDay — what comes across, what doesn't, and why.
eve.heroLede: EVE keeps your divers and their cards on a Windows PC in the back office. Here's how to get that data out of EVE yourself and bring your people, cards, and rental sizes into DiveDay — with a plain account of what makes the trip and what stays behind.

context.item1: EVE (from Integrated Scuba Systems) is the desktop shop-management system PADI retailers ran for years, and DiveShop360 acquired it in 2023. If you're planning a move off it, this guide is about the practical part: getting your people and their cards out of EVE and into DiveDay.
context.item2: The part that makes leaving feel risky is real: EVE stores its data in a database on your own PC, and shops report that years of purchase and service history are hard to pull out cleanly. DiveDay's import is deliberately not trying to move all of that. It moves the thing you actually need on day one — your roster, their certification cards, and their rental sizes — so your people are trip-ready from the first booking (see what comes across below), and the history stays where it already is.
context.item3: One rule we won't bend: you export your own file from your own EVE install. DiveDay never logs into EVE and never reaches across to another system to pull your data — that's your data to hand us, not ours to take.

eve.exportHeading: Get your data out of EVE
eve.exportIntro: EVE runs on Windows, so this happens on the back-office PC where EVE is installed — not on a website. The goal is a spreadsheet of your customers and their certification cards. Exact menu labels shifted across EVE versions, so treat these as the shape of the path, not word-for-word buttons.

step1.title: Open EVE on the shop PC and sign in with a manager account
step1.detail: Reporting and exports live in the back office, behind a manager or owner login — not the point-of-sale till. Use the PC where EVE actually holds its database.

step2.title: Open the customer list or a customer/certification report
step2.detail: Find the area that lists every customer with their certification details — usually under a Customers or Reports menu. You want the full roster, not a single record.

step3.title: Widen the range to all customers, all time
step3.detail: If the list or report asks for a date range or an active-only filter, set it as broad as it goes so recent-only or lapsed customers aren't quietly left out.

step4.title: Export to Excel or CSV and save it
step4.detail: EVE's lists and reports export to a spreadsheet — choose CSV if it's offered, or export to Excel and use File → Save As → CSV. Save it somewhere you'll find it, like the desktop.

step5.title: Do the same for certifications if they're a separate report
step5.detail: If cards (agency, level, card number) live in their own report rather than on the customer list, export that too. A card number is what lets DiveDay bring a card across at all.

step6.title: Can't reach the export? Ask EVE's current owner
step6.detail: If your license has lapsed or the export is greyed out, DiveShop360 now owns EVE and can produce a customer and certification export for you. Ask in writing and keep the file — that file is all DiveDay needs.

exportNotes.note1: Do this while your EVE install still opens and your license is active — a working export today beats chasing it later.
exportNotes.note2: Your column headings don't have to match anything. DiveDay recognizes the common names EVE and every other system use, and shows you exactly how each column mapped before you commit.
exportNotes.note3: If EVE will give you a sales or booking report as well, take it — a file with one row per booking brings your regulars' visit history across, so a fifteen-year customer doesn't arrive looking brand new. Register receipts and repair tickets stay in EVE; see the scope table below.

context.item3: One rule we won't bend: you export your own CSV from your own DiveShop360 account. DiveDay never signs into DiveShop360 and never reaches across to pull your data — that's your data to hand us, not ours to take.

context.item1: FareHarbor is an online booking platform for tours, activities, and rentals — owned by Booking Holdings, the company behind Booking.com — and plenty of dive shops run their storefront on it. It's genuinely good at that job: guests book and pay online, and its distribution network puts your trips in front of hotels, concierges, and resellers you'd never reach on your own. We're not here to talk you out of any of that.
context.item2: What it isn't is dive software. FareHarbor makes no claim to certification gating, medical waivers that fail closed, rental-gear fit, or a boat manifest built for a roll call — because it's a general booking engine, not a dive shop's back office. about.heroTitle: Your season doesn't hang on us.
about.phoneFrameLabel: A captain running roll call in DiveDay from the phone's offline copy.
about.heroDescription: Payments run through your own Stripe account, your records download as one ZIP any day, and roll call works on a phone with no signal. Divers build DiveDay — and everything below is either something you can go and try in the next few minutes, or something we're telling you outright that we don't do.
about.founderP1: A dive shop owner walked me through an ordinary day: a whiteboard, a clipboard, a hand-updated spreadsheet, and a few apps that don't talk to each other. He was paying for it twice — once in software, again in the hours it pulled from his divers.
about.founderP2: That's the pattern: an entire industry running on software nobody built for it — dated at best, hostile at worst, built for a back office, not a wet dock. Shops keep the whiteboard and clipboard because paper never crashes, never logs you out, never needs five taps with wet hands.
about.founderP3: DiveDay closes that gap: software fast, clear, and forgiving enough that a crew reaches for it unprompted — built from watching how a boat day runs, not a spec written far from the water. If your team wouldn't open it on a busy morning, it hasn't done its job.
about.runP1: Write in about a bad morning at the counter, a bug, or a question — a real person reads it and helps, not a form that asks you to attach a screenshot before anyone looks.
about.runP2: Pricing works the same way: the whole of it is on one page, and you can read every line of it without talking to anyone here first.
about.rulesTitle: Four rules, and you can check every one.
about.rulesDescription: These aren't promises. Each one is something you can go and prove wrong in the demo, in about a minute.

survivesDock.title: It has to survive the dock.
survivesDock.body: Wet hands, bright sun, one bar of signal, a boat that's already late. If a screen only works sitting down in an office, it hasn't been finished.
survivesDock.check: save a manifest to your phone, turn the network off, and run roll call anyway.

noSilentPasses.title: No silent passes.
noSilentPasses.body: Software that quietly waves a diver through because a field was blank is worse than paper. When DiveDay can't verify something, it says so and stops — and says which thing.
noSilentPasses.check: open the blockers queue and read why each name is on it.

onePrice.title: One price, no seats.
onePrice.body: Everything the product does is in the price. There is no tier that hides the feature you actually need, and nobody here is paid to sell you more of it.
onePrice.check: read the pricing page. It's one number and one list.

yourRecords.title: Your records are yours.
yourRecords.body: The export isn't a retention lever we release when you threaten to leave. It's a button, it works on day one of a trial, and it hands back documented files rather than a proprietary dump.
yourRecords.check: start a trial and download the ZIP before you've entered anything.

about.plainlyDescription: You'd find these out anyway. Better now than after you've moved a season of bookings.

new.title: DiveDay is new.
new.body: You'd be among the first shops on it. That's why the demo is a working shop instead of a sales call, and why the export button works on your first day.

feeAnchor.title: A flat price, or a cut of every seat you sell.
feeAnchor.body: Two of the booking channels a dive shop gets offered charge by the booking instead of by the month. Here is what each of them says about its own price — not what any shop ends up paying, which we have no way to know and are not going to guess.
feeAnchor.rezdy: {competitor}'s current published pricing is a monthly subscription plus 3% of every online booking. The option with no monthly fee still takes the 3%.
feeAnchor.fareharbor: {competitor} publishes no rate at all. It charges nothing monthly and takes a fee on every booking, added to your guest's checkout price, for as long as you use it; third parties report that fee at around 6%.
feeAnchor.ours: DiveDay takes no cut of a booking. Checkout runs through your own Stripe account, and what you pay us is the price on the card above — the same number in a busy August as in a quiet January.
feeAnchor.sourcesNote: Both descriptions come from the switching guides, where each one is cited to the incumbent's own pages.

dataExit.title: The exit is a button, not a support ticket.
dataExit.body: Every diver, booking, signed waiver and payment history, as documented CSVs — plus every photo the shop stored, as real files rather than links. One ZIP, downloaded by the shop's owner from Settings, on any day including the first day of a trial.
dataExit.honestNote: Two things it will not hand over, and the screen says so: login accounts with their password hashes, and the push credentials tied to a particular phone. Neither means anything in another system, and a file of password hashes is not something a download button should produce.

pricing.faqTitle: The questions that actually decide it.

whatIncluded.question: What is included?
whatIncluded.answer: The founding-shop price covers every currently available DiveDay workflow, from public bookings through the offline-ready boat manifest. It is not a collection of separate per-feature add-ons.

billing.question: How does billing work?
billing.answer: Month to month, per location. Cancel whenever you like and leave with your shop's records through the export button — no setup fee and no annual contract.

trialMeaning.question: What does "trial" mean right now?
trialMeaning.answer: Starting a shop is free for 3 weeks, no card required.

seeBefore.question: Can I see it before I commit?
seeBefore.answer: Yes. Open the live demo to see the day as the shop owner, an instructor, a divemaster, the captain, or a diver — it's a shop already full of sample trips. Or start a trial shop of your own: it begins empty, ready for your first trip.

offline.question: Does the manifest work offline?
offline.answer: Yes. The crew saves the manifest to their phone before leaving the dock. Departure and after-dive roll calls work from that copy, the screen always shows how fresh it is, and when service returns DiveDay checks every change against the live manifest before it counts.

dataIfNotWorking.question: What happens to my records if I leave?
dataIfNotWorking.answer: You leave with your shop's records, whenever you choose. {claim} {terms}

switching.question: What does switching to DiveDay actually involve?
switching.answer: Export a spreadsheet of customers from your current system, and DiveDay's importer brings in your divers, cards, and rental sizes — showing exactly what will happen before anything is saved. Step-by-step guides cover {competitors}.

agency.question: Does DiveDay connect to PADI or SSI?
agency.answer: No agency lets software verify a C-card automatically, so DiveDay doesn't pretend. A photo goes on the diver's profile once; staff confirm it with the agency, and it stays with them for good. Courses arrive as your shop's copy of the agency catalog — you set prices and visibility.

pos.question: Does DiveDay replace my POS?
pos.answer: No — keep your register. DiveDay runs the water side: bookings, courses, readiness, prep, and the boat, paid through your own Stripe account. Add a retail line to an order, but there's no register or stock count here — we'd rather say so plainly.

whyFounding.question: Why be a founding shop?
whyFounding.answer: Because early shops steer — what your crew runs into shapes what ships next. Founding shops also lock in today's price for two years, and every new feature lands in the one plan there is, with no higher tiers to move things into.

multipleLocations.question: What about multiple locations?
multipleLocations.answer: Each DiveDay shop runs one location today. If you operate more than one location, email {email} — we'd rather build that with you than pretend it's already here.
